result: Mitochondria are ancient organelles derived from α-proteobacteria that are present in almost all eukaryotes and perform diverse functions including biosynthesis, catabolism, ion storage, apoptosis regulation, and energy production. These functions vary substantially across eukaryotic lineages.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are well-established facts about mitochondrial origin and function, supported by appropriate citations to the literature (Gray 2012, Sagan 1967, McBride et al. 2006, van Dooren et al. 2006, Zíková et al. 2016, Chernikova et al. 2011). These represent accepted scientific knowledge rather than novel findings from this study.

result: Apicomplexans are medically important intracellular parasites including T. gondii, which chronically infects approximately one-third of the world's adult population and can cause severe disease in immunocompromised individuals. T. gondii serves as a tractable genetic model for apicomplexan biology.
evaluation: Claims C10-C16 provide established background on apicomplexan parasites and T. gondii, supported by citation to Montoya and Liesenfeld 2004. These are well-documented facts that establish the biological and medical context for the study.

result: Apicomplexan mitochondria are critical for parasite survival and are targeted by important drugs. These organelles contain core mitochondrial processes, though the mitosome of C. parvum is highly reduced, lacking a TCA cycle but retaining iron-sulfur cluster synthesis capacity.
evaluation: Claims C17-C25 describe established features of apicomplexan mitochondria, supported by appropriate citations (Doggett et al. 2012, Phillips et al. 2008, Srivastava et al. 1999, Seeber et al. 2008, van Dooren et al. 2006, Mogi and Kita 2009). These provide essential background for understanding the study's context.

result: Myzozoans (including apicomplexans, dinoflagellates, and chromerids) possess mitochondria with unique features including fragmented ribosomal RNAs, lack of pyruvate dehydrogenase (replaced by repurposed BCKDH), phylogenetically distinct TCA cycle enzymes, and an ATP synthase lacking clear F0 component homologs.
evaluation: Claims C26-C35 describe established characteristics of myzozoan mitochondria, supported by multiple citations (Cavalier-Smith and Chao 2004, Moore et al. 2008, Danne et al. 2013, Jacot et al. 2016, Feagin et al. 2012, Foth et al. 2005, Oppenheim et al. 2014, Ke et al. 2015, MacRae et al. 2013, MacRae et al. 2012, Balabaskaran Nina et al. 2011, Sturm et al. 2015). These establish the unique biology of the study system.

result: Two complementary spatially-restricted biotin tagging approaches (mtAPEX and mtBirA*) were successfully established in T. gondii, with both constructs localizing to the mitochondrion and specifically labeling mitochondrial matrix proteins as demonstrated by detection of mtHsp60 but not cytochrome c.
evaluation: Claims C36, C44-C52 describe the successful implementation of mtAPEX and mtBirA* approaches, supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 1A-B), western blots (Figure 1C-D, 1H), and avidin labeling (Figure 1E-G). The specificity for matrix proteins is demonstrated by detection of matrix marker mtHsp60 but not intermembrane space marker cytochrome c in bound fractions.

result: The study identified over 400 putative mitochondrial matrix proteins in T. gondii using quantitative proteomics: 213 proteins in mtAPEX samples, 369 in mtBirA* samples, with 161 proteins common to both proteomes (421 total unique proteins).
evaluation: Claims C37, C53, C134 report the primary proteomic findings, supported by volcano plots (Figure 2A-B) and Venn diagram (Figure 2C). The statistical cutoffs (p<0.001, log2 fold change ≤−2.5) are clearly defined. The identification of ~400 proteins represents a major achievement in defining the T. gondii mitochondrial proteome.

result: Many identified mitochondrial proteins have no ascribed function or clear homology to proteins in well-characterized eukaryotes like yeast, and most are important for parasite growth and survival.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by phylogenetic analyses (Figure 4) and phenotype score data from Sidik et al. 2016 (Figure 4A, 4D). The finding that 35% of proteins are critical and 39% are important for growth (C85-C86) supports the claim that most are important for parasite survival.

result: Approximately 40% of proteins in the T. gondii mitochondrial proteome had strongly predicted N-terminal targeting sequences (probability >0.9), with a further ~20% having moderately predicted targeting sequences (probability 0.5-0.9).
evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by MitoProt II predictions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1. However, the authors appropriately note that ~40% had low probability scores, suggesting either false positives or that MitoProt II may not be suitable for T. gondii proteins, as it was not trained on this organism.

result: The mitochondrial proteome showed greatest enrichment in TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and pyruvate metabolism proteins, and identified all subunits of BCKDH, all TCA cycle enzymes, all Fe-S cluster synthesis proteins, and all nuclear-encoded subunits of respiratory complexes III and IV.
evaluation: Claims C56-C64 are supported by metabolic pathway enrichment analysis and the metabolic map in Figure 2D. The comprehensive identification of expected mitochondrial pathways validates the proteome's quality and coverage. The identification of 4/7 coenzyme Q synthesis enzymes and 2/3 heme synthesis proteins indicates good but incomplete coverage.

result: The proteome did not identify mitochondrially-encoded proteins (cytochrome b, CoxI, CoxIII), intermembrane space proteins (cytochrome c isoforms), or the ε subunit of ATP synthase F1 component.
evaluation: Claims C65-C67 acknowledge limitations of the approach. The authors provide plausible explanations for missing mitochondrially-encoded proteins (hydrophobicity, inaccessibility to biotinylation, potential sequence errors). The absence of cytochrome c is expected given its intermembrane space localization, validating the matrix-specific labeling.

result: The mitochondrial proteome identified 97 out of 111 proteins (87%) that previous studies had experimentally localized or predicted to localize to the mitochondrion.
evaluation: Claim C68 demonstrates high coverage by comparison with previously known mitochondrial proteins. The 87% coverage rate indicates good sensitivity of the approach, though the basis for the denominator (111 proteins) should be more clearly defined.

result: Experimental localization of 27 selected uncharacterized proteins showed that 22 (81%) localized to the mitochondrion, with all 13 proteins from both proteomes localizing to mitochondria, but only 4/8 mtBirA*-only proteins doing so, indicating more false positives in the mtBirA*-only dataset.
evaluation: Claims C69-C73 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3. The differential validation rates (100% for shared proteins, 83% for mtAPEX-only, 50% for mtBirA*-only) provide important quality metrics and justify the authors' categorization of proteins as 'likely' vs 'possible' mitochondrial proteins. This represents rigorous experimental validation.

result: Phylogenetic analysis revealed that 71% of T. gondii mitochondrial proteins have homologs in P. falciparum, 61% in B. bovis, 28% in C. parvum, and 83% in V. brassicaformis.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by reciprocal BLAST searches shown in Figure 4A. The lower percentage in C. parvum (28%) is consistent with its reduced mitosome, while the high percentage in chromerid V. brassicaformis (83%) suggests conservation of mitochondrial biology in the myzozoan lineage.

result: Orthology analysis revealed 86 proteins unique to T. gondii and coccidians, 243 with orthologs in non-apicomplexan eukaryotes, and 89 found only in apicomplexans/chromerids. 51% of the proteome lacks orthologs in animals, of which 56% have orthologs in other apicomplexans/chromerids.
evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are supported by orthology analysis shown in Figure 4B-C. These findings reveal substantial novelty in the T. gondii mitochondrial proteome, with approximately half lacking animal orthologs. This has important implications for drug target identification.

result: Phenotype analysis showed that 35% of mitochondrial proteins are critical and 39% are important for parasite growth, with ~75% of proteins with orthologs in other apicomplexans being important or critical, and over 80% of apicomplexan/chromerid-conserved proteins being important or critical.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 are supported by phenotype score analysis from Sidik et al. 2016, shown in Figure 4A and 4D. The high percentage of important/critical proteins validates the biological significance of the identified proteome and suggests that even lineage-specific proteins are functionally important.

result: Proteins restricted to coccidians or apicomplexans/chromerids were just as likely to be important for parasite growth as proteins conserved across eukaryotic evolution, suggesting that derived or unique features of T. gondii mitochondria are critical for parasite survival, contrasting with the general T. gondii proteome.
evaluation: Claims C151-C153 are supported by phenotype score analysis in Figure 4D and comparison with Sidik et al. 2016. This is a surprising and important finding that challenges the general principle that conserved proteins are more important for fitness. The contrast with the genome-wide pattern adds significance to this observation.

result: TgApiCox25 has a predicted molecular mass of 25 kDa and localizes to the mitochondrion.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are supported by sequence analysis and immunofluorescence data in Figure 3R. This establishes the basic characterization of the protein selected for detailed functional analysis.

result: ATc-regulated knockdown of TgApiCox25 resulted in substantial protein depletion by day 2 and severe growth impairment, which was rescued by constitutive expression of TgApiCox25. Interestingly, rTgApiCox25 parasites grew better than WT in the absence of ATc.
evaluation: Claims C92-C96 are supported by western blot (Figure 5A) and plaque assay data (Figure 5B-C). The complementation experiment (C96) provides critical evidence that the growth defect is specifically due to TgApiCox25 loss. The enhanced growth of rTgApiCox25 without ATc (C95) is an interesting observation that may reflect altered expression timing.

result: TgApiCox25 knockdown led to ~80% depletion in basal mitochondrial O2 consumption rates and depletion of maximal mOCR, but no increase in spare capacity, indicating TgApiCox25 is not a component of ATP synthase.
evaluation: Claims C97-C99 are supported by Seahorse XFe96 data in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2. The lack of increased spare capacity distinguishes TgApiCox25 from ATP synthase components and suggests a role in the electron transport chain. The statistical analysis using linear mixed-effects models is appropriate.

result: TgApiCox25 knockdown resulted in a slight increase in ECAR, no gross mitochondrial morphological defects, and was reversible with equivalent viability after 3 days of ATc treatment, indicating parasites remain metabolically active and viable despite mOCR defects.
evaluation: Claims C100-C105 are supported by ECAR measurements (Figure 5E), immunofluorescence (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A), and plaque assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B). These controls are essential for demonstrating that the mOCR defect is specific and not due to general metabolic collapse or cell death. The cycloheximide control (C102) appropriately shows what general metabolic failure looks like.

result: TgApiCox25 has an important, specific role in oxidative phosphorylation in T. gondii parasites.
evaluation: Claim C106 is a reasonable conclusion from the combined evidence showing specific mOCR defects (C97-C99) without general metabolic or viability defects (C100-C105). The specificity is well-demonstrated through appropriate controls.

result: TgApiCox25-HA exists at ~600 kDa when separated by blue native-PAGE but ~25 kDa by SDS-PAGE, indicating it is a component of a ~600 kDa protein complex in the parasite mitochondrion.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 are supported by blue native-PAGE (Figure 6A) and SDS-PAGE (Figure 6B) data. The difference between native and denaturing conditions clearly demonstrates that TgApiCox25 exists in a large protein complex, consistent with it being part of a respiratory complex.

result: Immunoprecipitation of TgApiCox25-HA identified 12 enriched proteins including three canonical COX subunits (TgCox2A, TgCox2b, TgCox5b), seven proteins with homologs in apicomplexans/chromerids, and one T. gondii-specific protein (TgApiCox16). All except TgApiCox16 are important for parasite growth.
evaluation: Claims C110-C116 are supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 6C, Table 1) and HMMER similarity searches. The identification of canonical COX subunits validates the approach, while the identification of novel ApiCox proteins is a major finding. The phenotype score data from Sidik et al. 2016 supports the functional importance of these proteins.

result: TgCox2a-FLAG exists in a ~600 kDa complex and reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrate that TgCox2a-FLAG and TgApiCox25-HA exist in the same complex.
evaluation: Claims C117-C120 are supported by blue native-PAGE (Figure 7A) and reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 7B). The reciprocal IPs with appropriate negative controls (TgAtpB, TgTom40) provide strong evidence for specific interaction. This validates the mass spectrometry findings.

result: TgApiCox25-FLAG and TgApiCox30-HA both exist in a ~600 kDa complex, and reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation demonstrates they exist in the same protein complex.
evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by blue native-PAGE (Figure 7C) and reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 7D). This provides additional validation of the complex composition and demonstrates that multiple ApiCox proteins are part of the same ~600 kDa complex.

result: TgApiCox25 and TgApiCox30 are components of the parasite COX complex, the terminal oxidase of the mitochondrial electron transport chain that facilitates O2 reduction.
evaluation: Claim C125 is supported by the combination of O2 consumption data (Figure 5D), complex size determination (Figures 6A, 7A, 7C), co-immunoprecipitation with canonical COX subunits (Figures 7B, 7D), and mass spectrometry identification of COX subunits in the complex (Figure 6C, Table 1). The evidence converges to support this conclusion.

result: HHPRED analysis revealed that canonical COX subunits had expected homology to other eukaryotes, TgApiCox25 had predicted homology to Cox6a from Bos taurus, TgApiCox23 to Cox4 from Bos taurus, and ApiCox13 to human CDGSH iron-sulfur domain containing protein 3.
evaluation: Claims C126-C129 are based on HHPRED analysis. While C126 shows strong homology (probability >98.9%, e-value <6.6e-11), the predictions for TgApiCox25 (probability 90.9%, e-value 0.58) and TgApiCox23 (probability 95.57%, e-value 0.0057) are weaker. The ApiCox13 prediction is strong (probability 99.95%, e-value 3.1e-31). These structural predictions require experimental validation, particularly for the weaker predictions.

result: TgApiCox25 knockdown led to depletion of TgCox2a-FLAG and the ~600 kDa COX complex, with appearance of a ~400 kDa complex containing TgCox2a, indicating TgApiCox25 has an important role in COX complex integrity, stability and/or assembly.
evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by western blot (Figure 7E) and blue native-PAGE (Figure 7F) data. The appearance of a smaller ~400 kDa complex upon TgApiCox25 knockdown is particularly informative, suggesting either loss of a module or an assembly intermediate. This provides mechanistic insight into TgApiCox25 function.

result: TgApiCox25 is an important component of the parasite COX complex, and numerous other apicomplexan-specific components of COX were identified, indicating that apicomplexan COX and mitochondria differ substantially in protein composition from their hosts.
evaluation: Claims C40-C43 represent the major conclusions of the study, supported by the combined evidence from functional characterization (Figures 5-7), proteomic identification (Figure 6C, Table 1), and phylogenetic analysis (Table 1, Figure 4). The identification of 11 ApiCox proteins with limited homology outside myzozoans supports the conclusion of substantial divergence.

result: The T. gondii mitochondrial proteome of ~400 proteins is slightly smaller than mammalian (495) and yeast (750-900) proteomes. Based on validation rates, ~80% of uncharacterized proteins likely localize to mitochondria, with 213 proteins considered 'likely' and 208 'possible' mitochondrial proteins.
evaluation: Claims C135-C138 provide appropriate context by comparing to other systems and categorizing confidence levels based on validation data. The estimate of ~80% true mitochondrial localization for uncharacterized proteins is based on the 22/27 validation rate (C69, C136), which is reasonable but based on a relatively small sample.

result: This is the first direct comparison of APEX and BirA* approaches in organellar proteomics and the first use of APEX in apicomplexan parasites. The approaches provide complementary information, with mtBirA* identifying more proteins but also more false positives than mtAPEX.
evaluation: Claims C139-C143 are supported by the comparative analysis of the two datasets (Figures 2C, 3) and validation experiments. The assessment of novelty (C139, C143) appears accurate based on the literature cited. The complementary nature of the approaches (C140) is demonstrated by the 161 shared proteins and unique proteins in each dataset.

result: Phylogenetic comparisons show extensive conservation between T. gondii and P. falciparum mitochondrial proteins, consistent with similar biochemical pathways. The high conservation with chromerids (83%) and presence of ApiCox proteins in chromerids indicates much mitochondrial biology was present in the free-living myzozoan ancestor.
evaluation: Claims C144-C149 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4A, Table 1) and appropriate citations. The interpretation that derived features were present in the myzozoan ancestor is supported by citations to Danne et al. 2013 and Jacot et al. 2016. This provides important evolutionary context for understanding apicomplexan mitochondrial biology.

result: Many T. gondii mitochondrial proteins (~40-50%) lack orthologs in animals. The T. gondii COX complex is ~600 kDa (larger than yeast/mammalian/plant complexes at 200-300 kDa) and contains 15-16 proteins, comparable to mammalian (13) and plant (10-12) complexes. However, only a few T. gondii COX proteins have obvious homologs outside myzozoans, suggesting high novelty or sequence divergence.
evaluation: Claims C150, C154-C165 are supported by orthology analysis (Figure 4B-C), blue native-PAGE (Figure 6A), mass spectrometry (Table 1), and HMMER searches. The larger complex size is well-documented, and the lack of homologs outside myzozoans is clearly demonstrated. The alternative explanations (novelty vs. divergence) are appropriately presented. Comparison with other systems is supported by appropriate citations.

result: This study highlights the divergence of mitochondrial proteomes across eukaryotes. T. gondii and apicomplexan-specific mitochondrial proteins are prime drug targets given their importance to parasite growth and absence from host organisms.
evaluation: Claims C166-C167 represent appropriate conclusions from the study. The divergence is well-documented through phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4), and the importance for growth is demonstrated by phenotype scores (Figure 4A, 4D). The drug target potential is a logical inference from the combination of importance for parasite survival and absence from hosts.

result: 161 proteins in the T. gondii mitochondrial proteome have homologs in yeast, of which 103 were predicted to localize to yeast mitochondria and 58 were not.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84 compare the T. gondii proteome to yeast. While the identification of homologs is straightforward, the high proportion (58/161 = 36%) of homologs predicted not to localize to yeast mitochondria is concerning. The authors note that 72% of these are from the BirA*-only dataset (which has more false positives), but this still suggests either false positives in the T. gondii proteome or genuine differences in subcellular localization between organisms. More analysis would strengthen this comparison.
